title: List
body:
A sequence of elements in a definite order, where you can insert and remove anywhere. The
[[Abstract Data Type]]; the [[Linked List]] is one way to build it and an [[Array]] is
another.

Operations the ADT promises, regardless of how it is built: insert, delete, find, traverse,
is-empty, length.

Unlike a [[Stack]] (LIFO) or a [[Queue]] (FIFO), a list does not restrict *where* you may
touch it. That freedom is exactly what makes it more expensive: a stack only ever changes at
one end, a list can change anywhere, so the implementation has to be able to reach the middle.

The special cases worth their own names are the empty list (`head == NULL`) and the
[[Singleton List]]. Every insert and delete function has to handle both, and forgetting them
is where the [[Runtime Errors|crash]] comes from.

Python's `list` is this ADT with the [[Implementation]] hidden, which is what
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]] used it as; see [[Python List]] for what that concrete type
does that a C [[Array]] does not. Building one by hand here, and then analysing it in
[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]], is the point of the exercise.
